title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
one_liner: By repeatedly applying an autoencoder's encoding-decoding map, you can see where learned data points naturally settle, revealing whether the model memorized or truly understood.
lead: An autoencoder learns to squash images into a small list of numbers (the compressed representation) and then decompress them back. Researchers discovered that when you repeatedly feed those numbers through the encoder-decoder cycle without any new training, the numbers drift toward fixed resting points, called attractors. These attractors reveal whether the model learned to generalize (understand patterns broadly) or just memorized specific training images.

paras: Autoencoders compress images into compact codes. You train one and watch test accuracy climb. But you cannot see inside: did the model memorize exact training images, or did it learn general patterns it can apply to new images?

A naive approach: just look at test loss. Low test loss means it learned something, right? Not quite. A model can cheat by memorizing training data and still score decently on a held-out test set through luck. You need a way to peek directly at what the model absorbed.

callout.html: Reuse the autoencoder's own encoder and decoder: apply the encode-then-decode cycle over and over without training, and watch where each code drifts. The destination point it reaches tells you whether that example was truly learned or memorized.

panels.title: 1. Start with an image
panels.caption: Feed a real training image into the encoder.

panels.title: 2. Squeeze and expand once
panels.caption: Encoder produces a latent code; decoder reconstructs it. Mismatch pushes code toward true data.

panels.title: 3. Repeat the cycle
panels.caption: Cycle again. Code drifts more. On the third cycle, drifts less.

panels.title: 4. Code settles to attractor
panels.caption: After many cycles, code stops moving. That stable point is an attractor.

panels.title: 5. Compare to training set
panels.viz_args: Attractor matches the original cat photo.
panels.caption: Attractor decoded looks like the training image—means that image was memorized.

steps.text: Start with the latent vector representing a training image.
Run it through the learned encoder and decoder one iteration.
Keep cycling until the code stops changing (reaches an attractor).
Convert the final settled code back to an image.
Check if the decoded attractor closely matches any real training image.

paras: The paper does not retrain the autoencoder. Instead, it reinterprets it as a dynamical system: a set of rules that make codes evolve over time. Specifically, the latent vector field (the rule that says where each code moves when you apply encode-decode once) was already embedded in the weights during training. The paper simply exposes it by iterating.

hidden.name: Memorization coefficient
paras: An attractor is the stable resting point a code reaches after many encode-decode cycles. The paper measures a hidden quantity: the memorization coefficient, computed as the cosine similarity (a measure of how much two numbers point in the same direction, from 0 to 1) between the decoded attractor and the closest training image.

If a decoded attractor looks almost identical to a training example (similarity near 1), the model memorized that image. If the decoded attractor differs from all training images (similarity near 0), the model generalized, extracting a true pattern not just copying specific pixels.

heat.caption: Darker means higher memorization coefficient (attractor more similar to a training image).

reads.html: Memorization coefficient tells you: if I run this code through encode-decode many times, how much does the final image look like something the model saw during training?

The memorization coefficient measures attractor-to-training-data alignment by comparing each decoded attractor to all training images; high values indicate memorized examples, low values indicate generalized patterns.

paras: An autoencoder is trained to reconstruct images: it squashes an image into compressed codes and expands them back, with a penalty for mismatch. That training process shapes the way codes move when you apply the encoder-decoder pair. Think of it as creating a terrain: some regions are stable resting points (attractors), and codes naturally roll toward them.

During training, the autoencoder learns weights that create this terrain. A bottleneck (a small compressed space) acts like a filter: it forces codes to compress. With strong compression and enough training data, two things can happen. One: codes learn to represent general patterns, and all similar images converge to the same resting point. Two: if the model is over-parameterized (has more capacity than needed), each training image can get its own tiny resting point, and the model memorizes.

By iterating the encode-decode map repeatedly, you are letting a code move until it stops changing. The destination (the attractor) reveals what the training actually embedded: if a memorized image's code settles to a point that decodes back to that same training image, the model memorized it. If a code settles to a point that differs from every training image, the model learned a general pattern.

math.words: Latent code after k iterations equals applying the encoder-decoder map k times in a row. Start with a code z, apply the map f (which encodes then decodes) repeatedly until the code stops changing.
math.equation: z_k+1 = f(z_k) = E(D(z_k)), where E is encoder, D is decoder, iterated until ||z_k+1 - z_k|| < tolerance
symbols: distance (how far apart two codes are)
when to stop: if code barely moves, it has converged

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: After one cycle: z_1 = f(z_0) = [4.8, 2.9, 1.95] — the code shifted slightly.
After two cycles: z_2 = f(z_1) = [4.76, 2.87, 1.94] — smaller shift, converging.
After 20 cycles: z_20 ≈ [4.75, 2.87, 1.94] — code is stable, attractor found.
The attractor is z* ≈ [4.75, 2.87, 1.94]. Decode it and compare to the original training image.

math.note: Each iteration moves the code until it stops at a stable point (an attractor), which the autoencoder's learned weights created during training.

charts.title: Over-parameterized (memorizing)
charts.note: Attractors closely match training images; model memorized specific pixels.

charts.title: Well-regularized (generalizing)
charts.note: Attractors differ from all training images; model learned patterns.

items.html: If the autoencoder's learned terrain is complex (many tiny resting zones) or the code drifts chaotically, iteration may not converge to a stable attractor within reasonable time. The bottleneck dimension k must be small enough to compress.
In a model with strong constraints on weight movement, many different training images may converge to similar attractors, making it hard to distinguish memorized vs. generalized patterns.

When detecting samples outside the training set, random noise codes may also converge to attractors, especially if the model was trained on noisy data. The method relies on distinguishing the paths codes take, not just where they end up.
The method requires an invertible encoder-decoder pair. Standard discriminative classifiers (image-to-label networks) are not invertible, so the approach does not apply directly to them.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train an autoencoder on MNIST (handwritten digits) with two different bottleneck dimensions: one small (k=2, forcing heavy compression and memorization) and one large (k=128, allowing generalization). For each bottleneck setting, pick 10 training images, compute their attractors by iterating 100 times, and decode each attractor. Measure the memorization coefficient by comparing each decoded attractor to the 5 nearest training images using cosine similarity. Plot memorization coefficient (y-axis) vs. bottleneck dimension (x-axis).
demo.closing: The plot must show a clear trade-off: smaller bottleneck means higher memorization coefficient (attractors match training images); larger bottleneck means lower memorization coefficient (attractors differ from all training images).
